\section[\hi{दोपहर} \hi{आधी} \hi{रात}]{\hi{दोपहर}, \hi{आधी} \hi{रात} — noon by an old clock, midnight fully transparent}

\label{lesson:HI-C17-dopahar-aadhi-raat}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Hindi's word for noon hides a whole traditional timekeeping system inside it — one very different from hours and minutes.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{दोपहर} — "two pahars"}
\textbf{\hi{दोपहर}} (\emph{dopahar}) = "\textbf{noon, midday}" — literally "\textbf{two} (\emph{do}) + \textbf{pahar}." A \textbf{\hi{पहर}} (\emph{pahar}, from Sanskrit \emph{prahara}) is a traditional Indian unit of time, roughly \textbf{three hours} long, with the day traditionally divided into eight \emph{pahars} (four for daytime, four for night), counted from sunrise. Noon falls right around the end of the \textbf{second} daytime \emph{pahar} after sunrise — so \emph{do-pahar}, "two pahars {[}in{]}," became the everyday word for midday. (This traditional pahar-based account is the standard one, though — as with any folk-timekeeping etymology this old — treat the exact number of pahars as the general shape of the story rather than a precisely dated fact.)

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{आधी} \hi{रात} — fully transparent "half night"}
\textbf{\hi{आधी} \hi{रात}} (\emph{ādhī rāt}) = "\textbf{midnight}," literally "\textbf{half night}" — \textbf{\hi{आधी}} (\emph{ādhī}, the feminine form of \textbf{\hi{आधा}}, \emph{ādhā}, "half") + \textbf{\hi{रात}} (\emph{rāt}, "night"). No erosion, no double meaning — structurally identical to Latin's \emph{media nox} and Spanish's \emph{medianoche}.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "pahar" — a traditional \textasciitilde{}3-hour watch — then "do-pahar," two pahars, noon{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "ādhī rāt" — half night, midnight{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the contrast — dopahar counts an old time-unit; ādhī rāt is plainly "half" + "night"{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} What does \textbf{\hi{दोपहर}} literally mean, and what's a \emph{pahar}? ("\textbf{Two pahars}" — a \emph{pahar} being a traditional \textasciitilde{}3-hour time-unit, with noon falling around the end of the second one after sunrise.) What does \textbf{\hi{आधी} \hi{रात}} literally mean? ("\textbf{Half night}" — \emph{ādhī} "half" + \emph{rāt} "night," fully transparent, just like Latin's \emph{media nox}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
